title: On the road
mission: Getting anywhere in Palestine is a language event: flagging the serveece, paying the أجرة, taking directions past the mosque, and the checkpoint with its procedural grammar — هوية، تصريح، تفتيش. This unit teaches movement the way it actually works, city names the way they're actually said.
sources: Forms cross-checked against Madrasa dictionary and Living Arabic Project (Levantine)
Urban Palestinian koine (Jerusalem/Ramallah); native-speaker review pending — low-confidence items avoided

lessons.title: The serveece
lessons.canDo: I can board a serveece, pay, follow the driver's patter, and get let off exactly where I want.

blocks.body: The serveece — the shared taxi running fixed routes — is Palestine's circulatory system, and it runs on formulas: في محل؟ قديش الأجرة؟ نزّلني هون. Ten words and you ride like a local. The imperatives you'll meet here are the unit's engine.

example.en: I'm waiting for the serveece at the station.

items.note: From English 'service' — the yellow shared taxi on a fixed route. Same institution as the Israeli שירות, same borrowed word.

example.en: The serveece station is next to the market.

items.note: Root ح-ط-ط 'to set down' — where things get set down. Semantic twin of תחנה but a different root (that one is from חנה, to encamp).

example.en: The serveece takes seven passengers.

items.note: From ركب, to ride — also מרכבה territory: the Hebrew chariot rides the same root.

cognate.note: Both descend from Aramaic אגרא (hire, wage — ultimately Akkadian). The Israeli toll-road אגרה and the serveece أجرة are the same ancient invoice.

example.en: How much is the fare to Jerusalem?
Is there a free seat up front?

items.note: Seats, time, people: إنت فاضي بكرا؟ — are you free tomorrow? Opposite of مشغول.

cognate.note: m-l-ʔ — full is full: مليان/מלא, and the square that was مليانة ناس in Unit 2 was מלאה אנשים.

example.en: The serveece is full — wait for the next one.
The road's been one traffic jam since morning.

items.note: عالطريق — on the way (this unit's name). Feminine in the dialect: الطريق مسكرة.

example.en: Drop me at the junction, please.

items.note: نزّلني هون! is THE serveece sentence. The doubled middle letter makes نزل (go down) into 'make go down' — same trick as خبّر from خبر.

example.en: Stop here, boss!

items.note: Same root as موقف (stop/parking) and واقف (standing). يا معلم to the driver — your Unit 2 'boss' usage, live.

cognate.note: From يا الله — 'O God (let's move).' Israeli Hebrew took it whole; you've said it your entire life. Now it drives the serveece.

example.en: Yalla — close the door!

blocks.title: Any room?
blocks.situation: Flagging a serveece from Ramallah toward Birzeit: the boarding ritual, the fare, the drop-off — every line is a formula you'll reuse weekly.

lines.speaker: راكب
lines.en: To the university? Any room?

lines.speaker: سواق
lines.ar: اطلع يا زلمة، في محل قدام.
lines.en: Get in, man — there's a seat up front.

lines.speaker: راكب
lines.en: How much is the fare?

lines.speaker: سواق
lines.en: Seven shekels.

lines.speaker: راكب
lines.en: Here you go. Wow, the serveece is packed today.

lines.speaker: سواق
lines.ar: الطريق كلها أزمة من الصبح، والناس مستعجلة.
lines.en: The road's been jammed since morning, and everyone's in a hurry.

lines.speaker: راكب
lines.en: Main thing is we arrive before noon.

lines.speaker: سواق
lines.ar: إن شاء الله. وين بدك تنزل؟
lines.en: God willing. Where do you want to get off?

lines.speaker: راكب
lines.ar: نزّلني عند المفرق، الله يعطيك العافية.
lines.en: Drop me at the junction — God give you strength.

lines.speaker: سواق
lines.en: You got it. Yalla — close the door!

questions.prompt: Where is the passenger headed?
How much is the fare?
questions.why: سبعة — single digit. If you heard a ـطعش or ـين ending, the number gym wants you back.

questions.prompt: Why is the road bad?
Where does he ask to be dropped?
questions.why: نزّلني عند المفرق — your Unit 1 مفرق, now from inside the serveece.

questions.prompt: «الله يعطيك العافية» is…
options: A blessing for someone working — the polite driver-thank-you
questions.why: Said to anyone mid-labor. The unwritten serveece exit line.

items.en: How much is the fare to Hebron?
The serveece is full — wait for the next one.
Is there a free seat up front?

points.explanation: Serveece Arabic is imperative Arabic: stop, drop me, get in, take. To a woman: وقّفي، نزّليني. Softened with لو سمحت or paid forward with الله يعطيك العافية — commands here are polite by formula, not by phrasing.

examples.en: Stop at the station, please.

examples.ar: اطلعي يا ستي، في محل ورا.
examples.en: Get in, ma'am — there's a seat in back.
Take a right after the mosque.

points.explanation: The motion pair of public transport: طلع gets you on (and up), نزل gets you off (and down). Same verbs run stairs, hills, and prices — الأسعار طلعت. With the doubling trick they push others: نزّلني، طلّعني.

examples.en: I got on the serveece at the station.
We got off at the roundabout and walked.

items.story: Aramaic אגרא — a wage, a hire — flowed into both languages: the Hebrew toll (אגרת כביש 6) and the Palestinian fare (أجرة السرفيس) are the same Akkadian-old payment, still collected on roads.
m-l-ʔ. Full in Hebron is full in Haifa: مليان/מלא. And when the driver says مليان and waves you off, the disappointment, too, is fully shared.
يا الله — 'O God, (let's move).' The single most successful Arabic export into Israeli Hebrew. You arrive at this word already fluent; the serveece just gives it a steering wheel.

lessons.title: Which way?
lessons.canDo: I can ask for directions and survive the answer — دغري, take a right at the mosque, it's opposite the spice market.

blocks.body: Palestinian directions don't use street names — they use the mosque, the pharmacy, the spice market, and the immortal word دغري: straight ahead. This lesson installs the six direction words and the بدّي machinery for saying where you're trying to go.

example.en: Go straight until the mosque.

items.note: From Turkish doğru — 'straight/true.' Also a personality: واحد دغري is a straight-shooter. The Ottoman Empire left, the word stayed.

cognate.note: y-m-n — identical, down to the politics: the right is ימין in the Knesset and يمين on the serveece.

example.en: Take a right at the pharmacy.

cognate.note: ś-m-ʔ-l — same left. Bonus quirk: Arabic شمال is ALSO 'north' (face east like the ancients — north is on your left). Hebrew kept שמאל for left only and built צפון for north.

example.en: The house is the third street on the left.

cognate.note: q-d-m — forward. The seat قدام and the cry קדימה share a root; so do قديم (what came before) and קדום.

example.en: The market is right in front of you.
The garage is behind the station.

items.note: From وراء. Pairs with قدام the way ورا السرفيس pairs with قدام السرفيس — back seat, front seat.

example.en: The khan is opposite the spice market.

items.note: You heard قبال الساحة in the pharmacy call. Same q-b-l family as קבלה — what faces you is what you receive.

example.en: Not far — five minutes' walk.

items.note: Every Palestinian distance is خمس دقايق. It is never five minutes.

cognate.note: Your Unit 2 قرايب were the near-ones; here's the adjective itself, doing geography instead of genealogy.

example.en: The station is close — opposite the bank.
I'm lost — where's the old town?

items.note: Also figurative, exactly like English: ضايع بالحياة. Admitting it is the fastest way to make a Palestinian friend.

example.en: Can you take me to the station?

items.note: وصل (arrive) doubled into 'make arrive' — the same engine as نزّل and خبّر. وصّلني = get me there.

blocks.title: Lost in Nablus
blocks.situation: A guy from Ramallah is lost in Nablus's old city and asks an elderly man — who delivers the classic, generous, landmark-by-landmark answer.

lines.speaker: شاب
lines.ar: عمي، عفواً — أنا ضايع. وين خان التجار؟
lines.en: Excuse me, uncle — I'm lost. Where's Khan al-Tujjar?

lines.speaker: ختيار
lines.ar: أهلين يا ابني. إنت مش من نابلس، صح؟
lines.en: Welcome, son. You're not from Nablus, right?

lines.speaker: شاب
lines.ar: لأ، أنا من رام الله. جاي أشتري كنافة وضعت.
lines.en: No, I'm from Ramallah. Came to buy knafeh and got lost.

lines.speaker: ختيار
lines.ar: ههه، عالكنافة بتضيع البلد كلها. اسمع:
lines.en: Haha — for knafeh the whole country gets lost. Listen:

lines.speaker: ختيار
lines.en: Go straight until the big mosque.

lines.speaker: شاب
lines.en: Straight to the mosque… OK.

lines.speaker: ختيار
lines.ar: بعدين خود يمين، وامشي شوي بالسوق.
lines.en: Then take a right, and walk a bit through the market.

lines.speaker: ختيار
lines.ar: بتلاقي سوق العطارين قدامك — الخان قباله بالظبط.
lines.en: You'll find the spice market in front of you — the khan is right opposite it.

lines.speaker: شاب
lines.en: So it's not far?

lines.speaker: ختيار
lines.ar: قريب يا ابني — خمس دقايق. وكل الكنافة عالحساب تبعي إذا ضعت كمان مرة!
lines.en: Close, son — five minutes. And all the knafeh's on me if you get lost again!

questions.prompt: What is the young man looking for?
Why did he come to Nablus?
questions.why: جاي أشتري كنافة — a fully legitimate reason to cross the West Bank.

questions.prompt: First instruction:
Where is the khan, exactly?
How far is it, allegedly?
questions.why: خمس دقايق — the national unit of optimism.

items.en: Take a right at the pharmacy.
The khan is opposite the spice market.
I'm lost — where's the old town?
Can you take me to the station?

blocks.title: Where do you want to go?

points.explanation: بدّي isn't a verb — it's a possessed noun ('my wish') that conjugates like one anyway: بدي، بدك، بدكي، بده، بدها، بدنا، بدكم، بدهم. After it comes a bare verb: وين بدك تنزل؟ Negative: ما بديش.

examples.en: Where do you want to go today?
We want to arrive before evening.
I don't want to get lost again.

points.explanation: The preposition على shrinks to عَ in speech and glues onto the article: عالجامعة، عالحاجز، عاليمين، عالقدس. You've been hearing it since شو صار — now you know why half the words seem to start with عال.

examples.en: Heading to the market — need anything?
Take a left; the house is on the right.

items.story: y-m-n, the right hand — identical in sound, sense, and politics. Even בנימין, son of the right hand, has his Arabic cousins (ابن اليمين). Directions don't get more bilingual than this.

Same left — with an Arabic bonus: face the sunrise like the ancients and your left hand points north, so شمال does double duty as 'north.' Hebrew split the jobs: שמאל left, צפון north. When a Palestinian says بلاد الشام's شمال, the compass is in the etymology.
q-d-m is 'forward/before' in both time and space: قدام the front seat, קדימה the battle cry, قديم and קדום the long-ago. One root, simultaneously a direction and a history.

lessons.title: At the checkpoint
lessons.canDo: I can follow the checkpoint's procedural language — IDs out, open or closed, inspection or not, permit shown — as it actually unfolds in a serveece.

blocks.body: The حاجز is where Palestinian daily life meets the occupation's paperwork, and it has its own compressed grammar: هويات يا شباب، مفتوح ولا مسكر، في تفتيش. This is procedural language — flat, fast, essential. Learning it is not banal: it's how millions narrate their commute.

example.en: Checkpoint ahead — get the IDs out.

items.note: Root ح-ج-ز, to block/reserve. Hebrew מחסום is a different root (ח-ס-ם) building the same word for the same thing — twin barriers. A حاجز طيار is a 'flying' (surprise mobile) checkpoint.

example.en: Got your ID? Without it you don't get through.

items.note: Literally 'identity' — the green (West Bank) or blue (Jerusalem) card that scripts a Palestinian's geography. The colors are a whole political vocabulary of their own.

example.en: The soldier asked for the ID and the permit.

items.note: Plural جنود. The everyday word — جيش (army) you'll formalize in Arc 2.

example.en: There's a long queue at the checkpoint.

items.note: From Ottoman Turkish tabur (battalion) — the army word that became everyone's waiting line. Where Hebrew says תור, Palestinian remembers the Ottomans.

cognate.note: f-t-š travelled through Aramaic פשפש — to rummage. Hebrew kept the rummaging (לפשפש בחפצים); Arabic made it the official noun on the roadside sign.

example.ar: في تفتيش اليوم، الطابور ماشي عَ مهل.
example.en: There's an inspection today — the line is moving slowly.
We waited an hour at the checkpoint.

items.note: You've heard استنّاني and استنى شوي since Unit 1 — here's the verb officially. Hebrew חיכה means this — while Arabic حكى means 'spoke.' The false-friend from Lesson 1, now with its real twin.

cognate.note: m-n-ʕ, to withhold: Arabic ممنوع is the מ-נ-ע of מניעה wearing a 'no entry' sign. The road sign ممنوع المرور is pure shared Semitic bureaucracy.

example.en: Passage through here is forbidden today.

cognate.note: مسموح (permitted, s-m-ḥ) sounds like שמח (happy, ś-m-ḥ). Different roots. At a checkpoint, hearing 'happy' when the word was 'permitted' is a serious comprehension bug — though being permitted does make people happy.

example.en: Are we allowed through or not?

items.note: لو سمحت — 'if you'd permit' — is this root being polite. سمح/ممنوع run the entire signage of daily life.

example.ar: بدنا تصريح حتى نصلي في القدس.
example.en: We need a permit just to pray in Jerusalem.

items.note: تصريح شغل, تصريح زيارة, تصريح علاج — the permit regime has a noun for every movement. Also 'a statement' in news Arabic — Arc 2 will reuse it.

example.en: We got through the checkpoint, thank God.

items.note: The Levantine 'pass through' — مرق من هون (came through here), بنمرق (we'll get through). The checkpoint's most hoped-for verb.

blocks.title: Checkpoint ahead
blocks.situation: A serveece slows down; the driver runs the routine. Procedural, calm, fast — exactly how the daily checkpoint sounds from the inside.

lines.speaker: سواق
lines.ar: يا شباب، حاجز قدام. طلعوا الهويات.
lines.en: Guys — checkpoint ahead. Get your IDs out.

lines.speaker: راكب
lines.en: Closed or open?

lines.speaker: سواق
lines.en: Open — but there's an inspection today.

lines.speaker: راكب
lines.en: Is the queue long?

lines.speaker: سواق
lines.en: A bit. Wait — five minutes and we're through.

lines.speaker: راكب
lines.ar: معي تصريح شغل، إن شاء الله ما في مشكلة.
lines.en: I've got a work permit — hopefully no problem.

lines.speaker: سواق
lines.en: ID and permit in your hand, and stay calm.

lines.speaker: راكب
lines.en: What's the soldier saying?

lines.speaker: سواق
lines.ar: بقول افتحوا الشبابيك. افتح يا زلمة.
lines.en: He says open the windows. Open up, man.

lines.speaker: راكب
lines.en: Done… we're through. Thank God.

questions.prompt: What does the driver tell everyone first?
The checkpoint today is…
What document does the passenger have besides his ID?
The driver's advice:
questions.why: خليك هادي — stay calm. The checkpoint's survival grammar in three words.

questions.prompt: What does the soldier want?
«مرقنا» means…
questions.why: مرق — the Levantine pass-through verb, and the sentence's entire emotional payload.

items.ar: بدون ____ ما بتقدر تشتغل في القدس.
items.en: Without a permit you can't work in Jerusalem.
We waited a full hour at the checkpoint.
Passing through here is forbidden today.
Thank God, we got through quickly today.
There's an inspection — the line is moving slowly.

blocks.title: States and existence: the checkpoint report

points.explanation: Checkpoint news comes in participles — little adjectives made from verbs: مفتوح open(ed), مسكر closed, واقف standing/stopped, ماشي moving. No 'is' needed: الحاجز مفتوح، الطريق مسكرة، الطابور ماشي. This is how road conditions are reported, person to person, all day.

examples.en: The checkpoint is open but the road is closed.
The serveece is standing at the station.
The line is moving — stay calm.

points.explanation: Existence is one syllable: في تفتيش (there's an inspection), ما في مشكلة (no problem), في محل؟ (any room?). You've used it since Unit 1 — now notice it carrying the whole checkpoint report: في طابور، في تفتيش، ما في مرور.

examples.en: There's a flying checkpoint past the junction.

examples.ar: ما في تفتيش اليوم، امرق دغري.
examples.en: No inspection today — go straight through.

items.story: m-n-ʕ, to withhold. Arabic stamped it on signs (ممنوع المرور); Hebrew kept it procedural (מניעה, אמצעי מניעה). Two bureaucracies, one root, the same closed gate.
Permitted (s-m-ḥ) vs happy (ś-m-ḥ) — different roots that collapsed into near-identical sounds. مسموح المرور does not mean the crossing is joyful. Though relative to ممنوع, it might as well.
p/f-t-ḥ — to open. الحاجز مفتوح and המחסום פתוח are the same sentence twice. The root even named a movement: فتح. Doors, checkpoints, politics — one verb opens them all.

lessons.title: The cities
lessons.canDo: I can catch Palestinian place names at speed — and the identity words built from them: مقدسي، خليلي، نابلسي، غزاوي.

blocks.body: Geography here is biography: where you're from explains your ID color, your accent, your كنافة loyalties. This lesson is the map as Palestinians say it — including الداخل, the Inside, and the distances that aren't about kilometers.

cognate.note: q-d-š — holiness itself. The Arabic name IS the Hebrew root: القدس is 'the Holy,' עיר הקודש word for word.

example.en: My sister lives in Jerusalem.

items.note: A Jerusalemite is مقدسي — a word carrying a specific ID card and a specific set of problems.

cognate.note: Two languages, one naming logic: Arabic الخليل 'the Friend' (Abraham, خليل الرحمن) and Hebrew חברון from ח-ב-ר, friend/join. Different roots, same idea — the Friend's city.

example.en: Hebron is the biggest city in the West Bank.

items.note: خليلي = Hebronite — nationally famous as sharp traders, and the butt of jokes they tell better themselves.

example.en: Nablus is famous for knafeh.

items.note: From Roman Neapolis — 'new city,' like Naples. Hebrew kept the biblical שכם. The adjective نابلسي certifies both people and cheese.

cognate.note: ʕazza — the same ancient name in both mouths; Hebrew עזה even hears 'strong' (עז) in it. The ع/ע is the same letter doing the same work.

example.ar: خالي في غزة — صار لنا سنين ما شفناه.
example.en: My uncle is in Gaza — we haven't seen him in years.

items.note: غزاوي = Gazan. One sentence of geography, a whole arc of this curriculum (Arc 3) of consequence.

cognate.note: The Holy Land's most famous false friend: Arabic لحم is meat, Hebrew לחם is bread — so it's House of Meat vs House of Bread (and possibly originally neither: the god Laḫmu). Same name, different dinner.

example.ar: بيت لحم جنب القدس، بس بينهم جدار.
example.en: Bethlehem is right by Jerusalem — but there's a wall between them.

items.note: Locals say تلحمي for a Bethlehemite — the بيت drops off.

example.en: Jericho is the oldest city in the world.

items.note: And the lowest. Winter destination — Palestinians go down to أريحا for warmth the way others go to the beach.

example.ar: أصل عيلتنا من يافا، من قبل الـ٤٨.
example.en: Our family is originally from Jaffa, from before '48.

items.note: عروس البحر — the Bride of the Sea. In the Ask Project clip you watched, half the grandparents answered with this word.

example.en: Our neighbor Abu Elias is from Haifa.

items.note: Abu Elias from Unit 2, finally placed on the map. With يافا وعكا واللد والرملة — the cities of the قبل الـ٤٨ sentences.

example.en: Hebron is the biggest city in the Bank.

items.note: ضفة = riverbank; everyone drops 'western' and says just الضفة. The trio that maps Palestinian speech: الضفة، غزة، الداخل.

example.en: Our relatives from the Inside visit us on the holiday.

items.note: How Palestinians say 'Israel-proper areas' without saying it: الداخل, the Inside — also أراضي الـ٤٨. فلسطينيي الداخل = Palestinian citizens of Israel. A one-word politics seminar.

blocks.title: A family across the map
blocks.brief: One man's autobiography told as geography: origin, displacement, study, work, the sister behind a permit, the uncle behind a fence. Listen once for the cities; listen again for what stands between them.
preQuestions: Which city is the family originally from — and since when?
Where does his sister live, and what does visiting her require?
Where's the best knafeh in the world, according to a clearly neutral source?

transcript.speaker: أبو يافا
transcript.en: Our family is scattered across the whole map.

transcript.speaker: أبو يافا
transcript.ar: أصلنا من يافا، من قبل الثمانية وأربعين.
transcript.en: We're originally from Jaffa — from before forty-eight.

transcript.speaker: أبو يافا
transcript.ar: سيدي وتيتاي طلعوا عالخليل، وأنا انولدت فيها.
transcript.en: My grandparents left for Hebron, and I was born there.

transcript.speaker: أبو يافا
transcript.ar: درست في نابلس — أحلى كنافة بالدنيا، بالمناسبة.
transcript.en: I studied in Nablus — best knafeh on earth, by the way.

transcript.speaker: أبو يافا
transcript.en: And I worked two years in Ramallah.

transcript.speaker: أبو يافا
transcript.ar: أختي ساكنة في القدس — بدنا تصريح حتى نزورها.
transcript.en: My sister lives in Jerusalem — we need a permit just to visit her.

transcript.speaker: أبو يافا
transcript.ar: وخالي في غزة. صار لنا سنين ما شفناه.
transcript.en: And my uncle is in Gaza. It's been years since we've seen him.

transcript.speaker: أبو يافا
transcript.ar: هاي فلسطين: ساعة بالسيارة — وعمر كامل من التصاريح.
transcript.en: That's Palestine: an hour by car — and a lifetime of permits.

questions.prompt: Where is the family originally from?
questions.why: من قبل الثمانية وأربعين — the sentence pattern from the grandparents clip.

questions.prompt: Where was the speaker born?
Visiting his sister in Jerusalem requires…
Who hasn't he seen in years?
questions.why: خالي في غزة — mother's brother, behind the fence. Unit 2's family tree meeting Unit 3's map.

questions.prompt: «ساعة بالسيارة وعمر كامل من التصاريح» means…
options: The distances are short; the permits make them long

questions.prompt: Play it. Which city did you hear?
questions.why: الخليل — the Friend's city. (الجليل, Galilee, is the sound-alike trap.)

questions.prompt: Play it. Which city did you hear?
Play it. Which place did you hear?

items.ar: أصل عيلتنا من ____، من قبل الـ٤٨.
items.en: Our family is originally from Jaffa, from before '48.
Jericho is the oldest city in the world.
Nablus knafeh is the best knafeh.
Our relatives from the Inside visit us on the holiday.

items.ar: بيت لحم جنب القدس، بس بينهم ____.
items.en: Bethlehem is next to Jerusalem, but there's a wall between them.

points.explanation: Add ـي to a place and you get its person (and its cheese): مقدسي Jerusalemite, خليلي Hebronite, نابلسي Nabulsi, غزاوي Gazan. It's the same machine as Hebrew's ־י (ירושלמי, עזתי). Identity in this dialect is one suffix away from geography.

examples.ar: هو خليلي بس ساكن في رام الله.
examples.en: He's a Hebronite but lives in Ramallah.
Nabulsi cheese is for knafeh only.
His wife is a Jerusalemite — she has a blue ID.

points.explanation: The two-part Palestinian where-from: residence (ساكن في) versus origin (أصلي من). After 1948 they rarely match, so the question من وين إنت؟ often gets both answers — and أصلاً does heavy lifting: I live here, أصلاً from there.

examples.ar: ساكن في عمان بس أصلي من اللد.
examples.en: I live in Amman but I'm originally from Lydda.

examples.ar: من وين إنتو أصلاً؟ — من حيفا.
examples.en: Where are you all from originally? — From Haifa.

items.story: q-d-š — the holy. The Arabic name of the city is simply the Hebrew root wearing a definite article: القدس / עיר הקודש. Whatever else the two languages dispute, they agree on what this city is made of.

Not a cognate — better: a translation. Arabic calls the city 'the Friend' after إبراهيم خليل الرحمن; Hebrew's חברון grows from ח-ב-ר, to befriend. Two roots, one nickname for one ancestor — and his tomb still anchors both names.

lḥm split ways millennia ago: bread to the Hebrews, meat to the Arabs. So Bethlehem feeds everyone differently — בית לחם serves bread, بيت لحم serves meat, and the original Laḫmu (if that's the source) was a god who needed neither.

ʕazza — one of the oldest continuously-spoken city names on earth, identical in both languages down to the pharyngeal. Hebrew folk-hears עז, strength, in it. Arc 3 of this course lives behind this word.

lessons.title: Road trouble
lessons.canDo: I can follow someone narrating road trouble — the jam, the flying checkpoint, the empty tank, the strike — and the workarounds.

blocks.body: Every Palestinian commute is a contingency plan. This lesson is the vocabulary of things going wrong — عجقة، إضراب، حاجز طيار — and of coping: the bypass road, the walk, the immortal عَ مهلك. It's also where you learn to be late in fluent Arabic.

example.en: There's a terrible jam at the junction.

items.note: The Levantine word — أزمة works too (you met it at the roundabout), but عجقة is the one with the exasperated hand gesture built in.

example.ar: بكرا إضراب عام — كل البلد مسكرة.
example.en: Tomorrow is a general strike — the whole town is closed.

items.note: From ضرب, to strike — same metaphor as English. The إضراب عام closes shops, schools, and roads — usually mourning or protest. Arc 2 vocabulary arriving early, because the road feels it first.

example.en: I'm almost out of petrol.

items.note: Same European loan in both languages — بنزين/בנזין. عالآخر — 'at the end' — works for fuel, patience, and months.

example.ar: كراج سرفيسات الخليل عند إشارة المنارة.
example.en: The Hebron serveece depot is by the Manara light.

items.note: French garage, twice borrowed: the repair shop and the serveece depot. الكراج is where journeys begin.

cognate.note: Bus route, phone line, written line — خط and קו carry the same triple load. خط رام الله–القدس is exactly קו ירושלים.

example.ar: خط القدس واقف اليوم بسبب الحاجز.
example.en: The Jerusalem route is suspended today because of the checkpoint.

items.note: And the Unit 2 callback: الخط مشغول — the line is busy.

example.ar: جربنا الطريق الالتفافي — طلع مسكر كمان.
example.en: We tried the bypass road — turned out closed too.

items.note: From لف, to wind around. طرق التفافية are the settlement bypass roads — occupation infrastructure with its own adjective. The Hebrew twin is כביש עוקף, same logic.

cognate.note: ʔ-ḫ-r — late is late: تأخير/איחור, and أخّر/איחר the verb. The apology texts write themselves in either language.

example.ar: في تأخير ساعة على كل الخطوط.
example.en: There's an hour's delay on all routes.

cognate.note: ʕ-g-l is the rolling root: Hebrew עגול round, עגלה the cart; Arabic عجلة the wheel and مستعجل the one rolling too fast. Hurry is circular motion in both languages.

example.en: I'm in a hurry — is there a faster way?

items.en: take it slow, easy does it

example.ar: عَ مهلك يا زلمة، الطريق وعرة.
example.en: Easy, man — the road is rough.

items.note: مهل is unhurriedness; عَ مهلك puts it on you, gently. The philosophical opposite of مستعجل, and the only sane response to عجقة.

example.en: I caught the last serveece to Hebron.

items.note: Its dark twin is فات: فاتني السرفيس — the serveece left me (literally 'passed me'). Between لحقت and فاتني runs the whole drama of the depot.

blocks.title: Stuck: a phone call
blocks.brief: A man calls his boss from inside the jam: the flying checkpoint, the fuel gauge, the failed bypass, the people who gave up and walked. One sentence of philosophy at the end.
preQuestions: What two problems hit at once (besides the jam itself)?

His closing motto — what does he tell himself (and you)?

A promise to be on time
questions.why: The road's philosophy in four words — followed by عَ مهلي وعَ مهلك.

items.en: There's a terrible jam at the junction.
Tomorrow's a general strike — everything's closed.
We tried the bypass road — closed too.
I caught the last serveece, thank God.
Easy does it, man — the road is rough.

blocks.title: Caught it, or it left you

points.explanation: Two verbs split punctuality. لحقت السرفيس — I caught it (I did something). فاتني السرفيس — it passed me by (it did something, to me). That dative ني on فات flips the blame: Arabic lets the bus abandon you. Use both daily; mean them.

examples.ar: لحقت آخر واحد، يا ساتر شو عجقة.
examples.en: Caught the last one — Lord, what a jam.
I missed the six o'clock serveece — waited an hour.

examples.ar: بدنا نطلع هلّق حتى ما يفوتنا.
examples.en: We need to leave now so it doesn't leave us behind.

points.explanation: مهل (unhurry) takes the same possessives as everything else: عَ مهلك (your pace), عَ مهلي (my pace), عَ مهلها. The road's politest imperative — and a complete philosophy when paired: عَ مهلي وعَ مهلك.

examples.en: Take the downhill slowly — the road is wet.

examples.ar: بشتغل عَ مهلي بس بخلص صح.
examples.en: I work at my own pace but I finish it right.

items.story: ʔ-ḫ-r: the late root. تأخّرت and איחרתי are the same confession; آخر and אחרון the same 'last.' Two languages, one shared relationship with the clock — complicated.

ʕ-g-l rolls: Hebrew got the circle (עגול), the cart (עגלה), even the calf (עגל — the round one). Arabic got the wheel (عجلة) and the person spinning too fast (مستعجل). Hurry, etymologically, is just going in circles.
Different ancient letters, same convergence: خط and קו both mean the drawn line, the bus line, the phone line. When خط القدس واقف and קו ירושלים מושבת, the two sentences are commuting together.

lessons.title: Review & free listening
lessons.canDo: I can follow real Palestinians describing checkpoint experiences — unscripted, at speed, with this unit's exact vocabulary.

blocks.body: The serveece, the directions, the حاجز, the map, the trouble. Now the proof: real people answering Corey's bluntest question — why are checkpoints humiliating? You'll hear هوية، طابور، تفتيش، استنى، تصريح used by the people who carry them daily. This is the unit's vocabulary with the politeness removed.

blocks.title: Real street: why are checkpoints humiliating?
blocks.brief: The Ask Project asks Palestinians the unit's hardest question. The answers are unscripted and fast, and they run on exactly the words you just learned: هوية، طابور، تفتيش، استنى، تصريح، جنود. You won't catch everything — catch the procedure words and the feeling words around them. This is what the lesson-3 dialogue sounds like when it's a life instead of a lesson.
preQuestions: Count the unit words you catch: هوية، طابور، تفتيش، استنى، تصريح — which comes up most?
Many speakers describe waiting. What units of time do you hear — دقايق؟ ساعات؟ من الفجر؟
Listen for one full sentence you understand completely, and write it down — that's your exit ticket from Arc 1's road.
